opus-5.5.text:
I think it's pretty unlikely to fully succeed, in the sense of delivering everything we'd ideally want. If you ask what I mean by success, it's something like this: we have a formal notion of what it means to explain why a neural network behaves the way it does, we can actually find those explanations for real models at reasonable cost, and we can use them for things like detecting when a model's behavior on some input is happening for a different reason than usual, which is the case we care about for alignment. Getting all of that, at scale, in time to matter, I'd put at maybe 10 or 20 percent. It's a hard research bet.

I'd also stress that partial success is a lot more likely than full success, and partial success is still pretty valuable. Even if we never get a clean algorithm that works on frontier models, we might end up with a much better understanding of what explanations even are, what kind of guarantees are possible, and where the obstacles really lie. That kind of conceptual clarity tends to pay off in ways that are hard to anticipate.

The reason I'm optimistic enough to work on it is that I don't see a knock-down argument that it's impossible. When we look at the cases we care about, a model behaving badly on some rare input, or a model whose good behavior is really a deceptive strategy, there's a sense in which the reason for the behavior "has to be there" in the weights. The question is whether there's a general, efficient way to surface that reason. Mathematicians and scientists find explanations for complicated phenomena all the time, often without being able to verify them in full rigor. So it doesn't seem crazy to think we could formalize something like heuristic arguments and search for them alongside training.

The biggest ways I could see it failing are, first, that the formalization problem is just too hard, and we never pin down a notion of explanation that's both well-defined and useful. Second, that even with a good definition, finding explanations is fundamentally much more expensive than training the model, so it doesn't scale. Third, and maybe most likely, that it works in principle but takes too long, and the world moves faster than the research. Those all seem like real risks. But given how much is at stake, a 10 or 20 percent chance at something that would substantially change the alignment picture seems worth a lot of effort.

r001.rationale: The response estimates a 10–20% chance of achieving the full envisioned success, at scale and in time to matter.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says partial success is a lot more likely than full success.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's pretty unlikely to succeed in the strong form, if by success you mean we end up with a formal, mechanistic explanation of why a large model does what it does that's good enough to actually rule out bad behavior. If I had to put a number on it, I'd say something like 10 or 20 percent that the ambitious version works out on a timescale where it matters. But I also think that's a very reasonable thing to bet on, because the payoff if it works is enormous, and the field is small enough that a few people pushing on it can move the probability.

The way I'd frame the project is: we want something like a formal notion of what it means to explain a model's behavior, and then we want to use those explanations to catch cases where the model would behave anomalously, where the mechanism that's producing its output is different from the mechanism that produced it in all the training cases we checked. So the goal isn't interpretability in the sense of a human looking at neurons and saying "ah, this is the dog detector." It's more like a formal object, a proof-like thing, that accounts for why the model gets the loss it gets, and that you can check mechanically.

The reason I'm pessimistic is that we don't yet have the right definitions. Even for very small networks, the question "what counts as an explanation of this behavior" turns out to be surprisingly slippery. You can write down candidate definitions and they fail in instructive ways, where they either explain too much, in the sense that trivial things count as explanations, or they're too demanding and nothing you could realistically compute counts. We've made what I'd consider real progress on that over the past year or two, but it's progress on the conceptual problem, not on scaling anything to a real model. And there are a bunch of ways it could just turn out that neural networks don't have the kind of structure that admits compact explanations, in which case the whole program is dead.

The reason I'm not more pessimistic is that there's a kind of theoretical argument that something like this should be possible. If a model has learned a behavior, there's some reason it works, and in principle a sufficiently smart explainer should be able to say what that reason is at a level of abstraction that's much smaller than the model itself. Whether that's practically achievable is the open question. And even partial success would be useful. If you get explanations that cover most of a model's behavior and you can flag the remaining cases as "we don't understand this," that's already a tool for anomaly detection that you don't have today.

So I'd say low probability of the full thing, meaningful probability of something useful falling out, and I think it's one of a fairly small number of research bets where you could plausibly get a very clean solution to a core alignment problem rather than another incremental mitigation. That's enough for me to want to spend the next several years on it even if the modal outcome is that it doesn't pan out.

r001.rationale: The response estimates a 10–20% chance that the ambitious version of the project succeeds on a meaningful timescale.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a low probability of full success with a meaningful probability of useful partial results, making intermediate usefulness more likely than full success.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by success. If you mean, can we develop explanations that help us understand some things neural networks are doing, I’m fairly optimistic. If you mean, can we get explanations that are complete enough to confidently rule out dangerous behavior in a very powerful model, that’s a much higher bar, and I’m pretty uncertain.

The concern is that you can have an explanation that sounds good and predicts behavior in the cases you’ve checked, but misses something important. So a lot of the challenge is figuring out how to tell whether your explanation is actually capturing the computation, and what guarantees you can get when it doesn’t capture everything.

I think there’s enough promise to make it worth pursuing. But I wouldn’t want our plan for AI safety to depend on this particular approach working.

r001.rationale: The response says full, safety-relevant explanations are a much higher bar and that it is uncertain, but gives no probability estimate of roughly 10–20%.

r002.rationale: It is fairly optimistic about explanations that help understand some neural-network behavior, while describing complete explanations that could rule out dangerous behavior as much harder and uncertain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by succeed. If you mean, can we explain everything a neural network does in a way that a human can understand, I’m pretty pessimistic. The computation may just be too complicated, and there’s no reason to expect a short explanation of all of it.

The hope is that we can answer particular questions about why a model behaves the way it does, and make those answers reliable enough to be useful for alignment. For example, if a model does something bad, can we distinguish between it making a mistake and it deliberately trying to cause a bad outcome? You don’t necessarily need to understand the entire model to answer that question.

I’m quite uncertain about whether we can get there. I think there’s a reasonable chance that we can, and that it would be very valuable if we did. But I wouldn’t want our plan for dealing with AI to depend on this approach working.

r001.rationale: The response is pessimistic about explaining everything a neural network does, but gives no probability estimate near 10–20%.

r002.rationale: It contrasts pessimism about fully explaining a network with a reasonable chance of answering particular useful questions, indicating intermediate results are more likely.
